title: Mixed Leibniz formula for a scalar frequency multiplier
statement:
Use $\mathbf R$ [def-weil-field], smooth Euclidean functions [def-sfb-smooth-real-manifold], and the coordinate partial-derivative convention in [def-sfb-symbol-pseudodifferential-operators]. Let $u,v,p,q\geq0$ be integers, let $h:\mathbf R^v\to\mathbf R$ be smooth, and let $a:\mathbf R^u\times\mathbf R^v\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(\mathbf C^p,\mathbf C^q)$ be smooth. Then $b(x,\xi)=h(\xi)a(x,\xi)$ is smooth and for every pair of multi-indices $\alpha\in\mathbf N^u$, $\beta\in\mathbf N^v$ one has
$$\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta b(x,\xi)=\sum_{\gamma\leq\beta}\binom\beta\gamma(\partial^\gamma h)(\xi)(\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^{\beta-\gamma}a)(x,\xi).$$
Here $\gamma\leq\beta$ means coordinatewise inequality, $|\gamma|=\sum_i\gamma_i$, and $\binom\beta\gamma=\prod_i\binom{\beta_i}{\gamma_i}$. The matrix norm consequently satisfies
$$\|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta b(x,\xi)\|\leq\sum_{\gamma\leq\beta}\binom\beta\gamma|\partial^\gamma h(\xi)|\,\|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^{\beta-\gamma}a(x,\xi)\|.$$

source.place: WANTED locally: Demailly, Differential and pseudodifferential operators on manifolds, §3.6–3.7, printed p.7: coordinate Leibniz formulas, including the scalar cutoff product in the proof of asymptotic expansions. Agent statement of the general matrix-valued mixed formula.

proof.text:
Put $E=\mathbf R^u\times\mathbf R^v$ and $H(x,\xi)=h(\xi)$. The projection $E\to\mathbf R^v$ and the inclusion $\mathbf R\to\mathbf C$ are continuous real-linear maps. The smooth composition and linear-map rules give a smooth complex-valued $H$, whose real differential on $(s,t)$ is $Dh(\xi)[t]$. Choose the standard matrix entries $a_{ij}$ of $a$. These are smooth complex-valued functions: each entry is a continuous real-linear coordinate projection. The scalar product rule gives smooth entries $Ha_{ij}$ and
$$\partial_e(Ha_{ij})=(\partial_e H)a_{ij}+H\partial_e a_{ij}$$
for every coordinate direction $e$, where $\partial_e f(z)=Df(z)[e]$. Smoothness in real coordinates is entrywise smoothness, so these are the entries of the smooth matrix-valued function $b$. This argument concerns all entries simultaneously and does not choose a nonzero entry; if $p=0$ or $q=0$, the matrix space is zero and smoothness and all later equalities are immediate.

source.place: Proof (3), supporting cutoff calculus in the existing prerequisite chain; agent-written detail: smoothness and first-order scalar product rule

proof.text:
Every iterated coordinate derivative of each entry of $a$ and of $H$ is smooth. Indeed the differential of a smooth map is smooth, and evaluation $L\mapsto L(e)$ is a continuous real-linear map, so compose these two maps and repeat. The chain rule also identifies
$$\partial_e\partial_f g(z)=D(Dg)(z)[e][f].$$
Apply symmetry of the second differential to any already differentiated smooth $g$, with $F=\mathbf C$ viewed as a two-dimensional real space and open domain $E$. It gives $\partial_e\partial_f g=\partial_f\partial_e g$. Thus adjacent coordinate partials can be exchanged; finitely many adjacent exchanges put any finite word of partials in the chosen coordinate order. The same reasoning applies to real-valued $h$. All hypotheses here are smoothness on the whole Euclidean domain, hence in particular twice continuous differentiability; no boundary or restricted-domain derivative is used.

source.place: Proof (3), supporting cutoff calculus in the existing prerequisite chain; agent-written detail: smooth partial derivatives and adjacent exchanges

proof.text:
For a finite ordered list $w$ of coordinate directions, let $P_w$ mean applying the listed partials successively, and let $w|S$ be its sublist at positions $S$. For each scalar entry $A=a_{ij}$ prove, by induction on the length $N$ of $w$,
$$P_w(HA)=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}}(P_{w|S}H)(P_{w|S^c}A).$$
For $N=0$ the single term is $HA$, since $P_{\varnothing}$ is the identity. Suppose the equality holds as an identity of smooth functions. Apply one further coordinate partial $\partial_e$. Differentiation passes through the finite sum by repeated use of the sum rule. Applying the scalar product rule to each summand gives two terms: one differentiates its $H$ factor, one its $A$ factor. The former is indexed by $S\cup\{N+1\}$ and the latter by $S$, now as subsets of $\{1,\ldots,N+1\}$. Every subset occurs exactly once, according as it contains the new position or does not. The inherited orders of both sublists are exactly their orders in $(w,e)$, so this is the asserted identity at $N+1$. All factors being differentiated are smooth by step 2. This induction proves the word identity, rather than assuming a higher Leibniz formula.

source.place: Proof (3), supporting cutoff calculus in the existing prerequisite chain; agent-written detail: induction for the finite-word product expansion

proof.text: Choose $w$ with $\alpha_i$ occurrences of each $x_i$ direction and $\beta_j$ occurrences of each $\xi_j$ direction. By step 2 its derivative is the displayed mixed derivative, regardless of the order in this list. The first-order projection formula in step 1 gives $\partial_{x_i}H=0$. If $S$ contains an $x$ position, commute that partial to act first on $H$; its factor then vanishes, and further derivatives of zero are zero by the constant-map rule. A surviving subset has only frequency positions. Let $\gamma_j$ count its positions in direction $\xi_j$. Then $\gamma\leq\beta$, its $H$ factor is $(\partial^\gamma h)(\xi)$, and its $A$ factor is $\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^{\beta-\gamma}a_{ij}(x,\xi)$. There are exactly $\prod_j\binom{\beta_j}{\gamma_j}$ such subsets: independently choose $\gamma_j$ of the $\beta_j$ labelled occurrences for every $j$. This uses the elementary counting definition of the binomial coefficient. Group the finite sum of step 3 by these counts. The resulting scalar identity holds for every entry, hence is precisely the claimed matrix identity. Empty lists and empty products give coefficient $1$, covering $u=0$, $v=0$, and $\alpha=\beta=0$.

source.place: Proof (3), supporting cutoff calculus in the existing prerequisite chain; agent-written detail: grouping the word expansion and eliminating spatial derivatives on the multiplier

proof.text:
Take norms in the matrix identity. For finitely many vectors $T_\gamma$, induction on the number of terms using $\|S+T\|\leq\|S\|+\|T\|$ gives $\|\sum_\gamma T_\gamma\|\leq\sum_\gamma\|T_\gamma\|$. Norm homogeneity gives
$$\bigl\|\tbinom\beta\gamma(\partial^\gamma h)(\xi)\,\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^{\beta-\gamma}a(x,\xi)\bigr\|=\tbinom\beta\gamma|\partial^\gamma h(\xi)|\,\|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^{\beta-\gamma}a(x,\xi)\|,$$
since the binomial coefficient is a nonnegative integer. Substitution gives the stated inequality. Only the triangle inequality and absolute homogeneity defining the matrix norm are used; no estimate of full Frechet derivative norms or extra symbol bound is required.
